To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effect of dietary protein and fat on plasma cholesterol in growing chickens depends on the dietary protein level and that the product of the essential fatty acid content of a fat x the total saturated fat content of that fat is not related to plasma cholesterol level in growing chickens.

The effects of dietary fat on plasma cholesterol in growing chicks are influenced by dietary protein level, and that a high protein diet is effective in reducing plasma cholesterol in the presence of a high fat diet.
the plasma cholesterol levels of chickens are affected by the level of dietary protein but not the source of dietary fat.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects on plasma cholesterol levels of 4 fats, each supplied at 2 levels of supplementation in a high and low protein diet.
the influence of protein and fat in the diet on the level of plasma cholesterol in the growing chicken.
the effects of dietary fat on plasma cholesterol levels in the growing chicken.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the level of dietary protein is the major determinant of plasma cholesterol levels in the growing chicken, and that dietary fats, including the essential fatty acids, are of minor importance.
the plasma cholesterol levels of growing chickens are not influenced by the type or level of fat in the diet, but are dependent on the protein content of the diet.
plasma cholesterol level in growing chickens is not influenced by dietary fat or protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of dietary protein level on the plasma cholesterol level of the chicken is not influenced by the type of fat fed.
the plasma cholesterol response to dietary fats is influenced primarily by dietary protein level, but that other factors are involved.
plasma cholesterol in the growing chicken was not affected by the level of dietary protein, the source or level of dietary fat, or the product EFA × TSFA of the fat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can’t use plasma cholesterol levels to predict atherogenic potential.
we should not rely on the cholesterol content of food to predict its effect on our cholesterol levels.
you can’t just eat a high-fat diet and expect it to lower your cholesterol.
